young.what: Muscles are stretchy bundles under your skin that are joined to your bones.
young.does: They pull on your bones to make you move.
young.funFact: You have more than 600 muscles in your body!

junior.what: Skeletal muscles are organs made of long muscle fibres, attached to bones by tough cords called tendons.
junior.does: Muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs: when one contracts, its partner relaxes.
junior.funFact: Muscles make up about 40% of an adult's body weight.
junior.details: Skeletal muscles are voluntary: you decide when to move them. Heart muscle and the muscles of the gut work automatically.

young.what: Your shoulder muscle is the round muscle over the top of your shoulder.
young.does: It lifts your arm up to wave, reach and throw.
young.funFact: It is shaped like a triangle, just like the Greek letter delta!

junior.what: The deltoid is the thick, triangular muscle that caps the shoulder.
junior.does: Its front, middle and back parts lift the arm forwards, out to the side and backwards.
junior.funFact: It is named after the Greek letter delta (Δ) because of its triangle shape.
junior.details: The deltoid is often used for vaccinations because it is a large muscle that is easy to reach.

young.what: Your biceps is the muscle at the front of your upper arm.
young.does: It bends your elbow to lift things up.
young.funFact: Make a muscle! That bump is your biceps.

junior.what: The biceps brachii is the two-headed muscle at the front of the upper arm.
junior.does: It bends (flexes) the elbow and turns the palm upwards. It works as a pair with the triceps.
junior.funFact: 'Biceps' means 'two heads': it starts from two points on the shoulder blade.
junior.details: Its tendon attaches to the radius, which is why it also helps rotate the forearm.

young.what: Your triceps is the muscle at the back of your upper arm.
young.does: It straightens your elbow when you push or throw.
young.funFact: It is your biceps' partner: when one pulls, the other relaxes!

junior.what: The triceps brachii is the three-headed muscle at the back of the upper arm.
junior.does: It straightens (extends) the elbow, doing the opposite job to the biceps.
junior.funFact: The triceps is bigger than the biceps. It makes up about two-thirds of the upper arm's muscle.
junior.details: Pairs of muscles that do opposite jobs, like the biceps and triceps, are called antagonistic pairs.

young.what: Your chest muscle is a big, flat muscle across the front of your chest.
young.does: It pulls your arms across your body, like when you hug or push.
young.funFact: It is one of the muscles that help you do push-ups!

junior.what: The pectoralis major is a large, fan-shaped muscle on the front of the chest.
junior.does: It pulls the arm forwards and across the body and turns it inwards.
junior.funFact: It starts on the collarbone, breastbone and ribs, but all its fibres meet at one tendon on the humerus.
junior.details: Underneath it lies a smaller muscle, the pectoralis minor.

young.what: Your tummy muscles are long, flat muscles down the front of your tummy.
young.does: They help you sit up, bend forward and keep your body steady.
young.funFact: These are the muscles people call a 'six-pack'!

junior.what: The rectus abdominis is a pair of long, strap-like muscles running down the front of the abdomen.
junior.does: It bends the trunk forwards and helps hold the organs of the abdomen in place.
junior.funFact: Bands of tendon cross the muscle and divide it into the blocks of a 'six-pack'.
junior.details: It also helps you breathe out hard and cough by squeezing the abdomen.

young.what: These muscles wrap around the sides of your tummy.
young.does: They help you twist and bend to the side.
young.funFact: Twist like a corkscrew. That's your side muscles working!

junior.what: The external obliques are broad, flat muscles on the sides of the abdomen.
junior.does: They twist the trunk, bend it sideways and squeeze the abdomen.
junior.funFact: Their fibres run diagonally downwards and forwards, like your fingers when you put your hands in your pockets.
junior.details: Beneath them are two more layers of muscle: the internal obliques and the transversus abdominis.

young.what: This big, kite-shaped muscle covers your upper back and the back of your neck.
young.does: It lifts your shoulders and helps hold your head up.
young.funFact: Shrug your shoulders. That's your trapezius!

junior.what: The trapezius is a large, diamond-shaped muscle covering the back of the neck and the upper back.
junior.does: It moves and steadies the shoulder blades (shrugging, squeezing them together and rotating them) and helps hold the head up.
junior.funFact: Its left and right halves together look like a trapezium, which is how it got its name.
junior.details: Sitting hunched over a screen for a long time can make the trapezius feel tight and sore.

young.what: This is a big, wide muscle on each side of your back.
young.does: It pulls your arms down and back, like when you climb or swim.
young.funFact: It is one of the widest muscles in your body!

junior.what: The latissimus dorsi is a broad, flat muscle covering the middle and lower back.
junior.does: It pulls the arm down, backwards and towards the body, which you use in climbing, rowing and swimming.
junior.funFact: Its Latin name means 'the widest muscle of the back'.
junior.details: It starts on the lower spine and pelvis and attaches to the humerus near the armpit.

young.what: This is the big muscle that makes up your bottom.
young.does: It helps you stand up from a chair, climb stairs and run.
young.funFact: It is the biggest muscle in your whole body!

junior.what: The gluteus maximus is the large muscle of the buttock.
junior.does: It straightens the hip by pulling the thigh backwards when you stand up, climb or run.
junior.funFact: It is the largest muscle in the human body.
junior.details: It helps keep your body upright and balanced over your legs.

young.what: These are the four big muscles at the front of your thigh.
young.does: They straighten your knee when you kick, jump and stand up.
young.funFact: 'Quad' means four, because four muscles work together here!

junior.what: The quadriceps femoris is a group of four muscles at the front of the thigh.
junior.does: Together they straighten (extend) the knee. One of them, the rectus femoris, also helps bend the hip.
junior.funFact: Its four parts are the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and vastus intermedius.
junior.details: All four muscles join into one tendon that holds the kneecap and attaches to the tibia.

young.what: These are the muscles at the back of your thigh.
young.does: They bend your knee and pull your leg back when you run.
young.funFact: Reach down towards your toes and you'll feel your hamstrings stretch!

junior.what: The hamstrings are a group of three muscles at the back of the thigh.
junior.does: They bend (flex) the knee and straighten the hip, working opposite to the quadriceps.
junior.funFact: You can feel their tendons as firm cords at the back of your knee.
junior.details: The three hamstring muscles are the biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus.

young.what: Your calf muscles are at the back of your lower leg.
young.does: They lift your heel so you can stand on tiptoe, walk and jump.
young.funFact: Stand on tiptoe and your calf muscles bulge!

junior.what: The calf is made mainly of two muscles: the gastrocnemius and the soleus underneath it.
junior.does: They pull on the Achilles tendon to raise the heel, pushing you off the ground with every step.
junior.funFact: The soleus works almost all the time you are standing, stopping you from tipping forwards.
junior.details: When calf muscles squeeze, they also help push blood in the leg veins back up towards the heart.

young.what: The sartorius is a long, thin muscle that crosses the front of your thigh.
young.does: It helps you cross your legs and bend your knee.
young.funFact: It is the longest muscle in your body!

junior.what: The sartorius is a long, strap-like muscle running diagonally across the front of the thigh.
junior.does: It helps bend the hip and knee and turn the thigh outwards, as when you sit cross-legged.
junior.funFact: Its name comes from the Latin word for 'tailor', because tailors used to sit cross-legged while sewing.
junior.details: It starts at the front of the hip bone and ends on the inside of the tibia, just below the knee.

young.what: Your chewing muscles are on the sides of your face and head.
young.does: They close your mouth tightly so you can bite and chew.
young.funFact: Clench your teeth and touch your cheek. You can feel them bulge!

junior.what: The masseter and the temporalis are the main chewing muscles.
junior.does: They pull the mandible upwards to close the jaw with great force for biting and chewing.
junior.funFact: For its size, the masseter is one of the strongest muscles in the body.
junior.details: The temporalis fans out over the side of the skull; the masseter runs from the cheekbone down to the jaw.

young.what: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle under your lungs.
young.does: It moves down to pull air into your lungs when you breathe in.
young.funFact: Hiccups happen when your diaphragm makes a sudden little jump!

junior.what: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen.
junior.does: When it contracts, it flattens and moves down, making the chest bigger so air flows into the lungs. When it relaxes, it domes up again and you breathe out.
junior.funFact: It is the most important muscle for breathing, and it keeps working even while you sleep.
junior.details: Hiccups are sudden, involuntary contractions of the diaphragm.

young.what: This strong cord joins your calf muscles to your heel bone.
young.does: When your calf muscles pull, it lifts your heel so you can walk and jump.
young.funFact: It is the strongest tendon in your body!

junior.what: The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon joins the calf muscles to the heel bone.
junior.does: It passes the pull of the calf muscles to the calcaneus, raising the heel when you walk, run and jump.
junior.funFact: It is named after Achilles, a hero from Greek myths whose heel was his only weak spot.
junior.details: Tendons join muscles to bones, while ligaments join bones to other bones.
